method: After freezing and replaying the pair, returned separately to Groningen’s 2026–27 poster and formal curriculum and independently recomputed the 180 EC allocation. Checked the 2 EC Monitor only once, reread Article 9.3 and separately verified BWB306’s 45 EC catalog condition. Reconsidered the current workbook’s anatomy, physiology, perception, movement-measurement tools and qualitative inquiry against the underlying university descriptions. Checked both UCR outcomes and the limits of the eight aligned rows, then checked the student-facing conditions and options against the frozen record. Worker A conducted both passes.
findings: The Dutch-taught Human Movement Sciences BSc is a 180 EC degree with a common curriculum. Articles 4.1 and 7.1 verify twelve 5 EC first-year components and the 120 EC post-propaedeutic curriculum. The 2026–27 poster distinguishes Movement Analysis 1 and 2, Skills Lab, Neuroanatomy 1 and 2, and Statistics 1, 2 and 3 where the public table repeats or mislabels entries. Eleven 5 EC courses, 3 EC orientation and 2 EC Bachelor Monitor account for 60 EC in the comparison’s second-year grouping. Monitor runs across years two and three and is counted once. Year three includes a genuine 15 EC minor, five 5 EC modules and a 20 EC research project. Articles 7.1 and 8.1 allow minor study, placement or study abroad, subject to applicable approval.

The first year introduces anatomy, general physiology, neurophysiology, biomechanics, motor control, mathematics, programming and research methods. Later courses add exercise testing, laboratory measurement, motor development, neuroanatomy and movement interventions. Article 5.2 gives the 45 EC first-year binding study advice threshold, and Art. 5.7 addresses access to later years. Article 9.3 requires all 60 first-year EC and 43 second-year EC by the graduation-project application deadline. The current BWB306 catalog instead lists 45 second-year EC and the same first-year requirement and deadlines (1 December for February, 15 July for September). The comparison explicitly distinguishes the sources and uses the stricter 45 EC for planning. The modeled 60 EC in year two satisfies either threshold. The project includes supervised research, a report and presentation.

Both plans develop body systems, neural control and perception and use statistics and research synthesis. The measurement plan advances from programming, mathematical methods and linear algebra to numerical methods, linear systems, probability, machine learning and computer vision. Feature tracking and signal processing are relevant tools for motion analysis, while specialist force, gait and exercise testing require different equipment and progression. The health and behavior plan develops psychopathology, psychological assessment, health psychology and lifespan development around activity and coping. Biochemistry supports metabolism. Sociology and qualitative methods add attention to social barriers and lived experience using interviews and thematic analysis. Philosophy of Mind contributes a conceptual account of the mind–body relation. The plan studies recovery-related questions within broader health psychology and makes no claim to therapist training or a dedicated sport-psychology sequence. The original second plan placed Image Processing in an unavailable term, and the same course set is infeasible even after rescheduling with the academic sequence constraints. Retaining vision in the measurement plan and refocusing three selections in the second plan gives each a defensible sequence. The eight shared rows describe focused overlap. Dedicated movement pathology, lab analysis, exercise testing, sport psychology and the compulsory project are shown separately. Lifespan development includes psychomotor development, but does not constitute a specialist motor learning course. A sport-performance and talent plan lacks cumulative exercise measurement and performance-specific training in the active workbook.
